text.p: Renaissance Energy Ltd, Canada's busiest oil and gas driller, was expected to post lower earnings in 1997 but higher cash flow, Renaissance Chief Executive Clayton Woitas said on Tuesday.
Woitas told Renaissance's annual meeting that high oil and gas prices in 1996 played a big role in last year's strong profit showing and that he expected commodity markets this year to remain weaker.
Renaissance, which earlier reported improved first-quarter results, was expected to pump out earnings of C$140 million this year, down from C$180 million in 1996, he said.
Cash flow was projected at C$600 million in 1997, up from C$573 million last year, he said.
Woitas said he expected oil and gas prices to be about 15 percent lower on average than last year, when the value of crude oil especially beat most expectations.

"We would view 1996 as being an exceptional year commodity price-wise," Woitas told reporters after the meeting. "It could be duplicated but we would sooner err on the conservative on assumptions and adjust upwards going forward."

Renaissance, which budgeted spending C$700 million to C$800 million drilling up to 1,800 wells in Alberta and Saskatchewan, should achieve average production of 92,500 barrels of oil and 450 million cubic feet of natural gas this year, Woitas said.
The company's output in 1996 was 71,921 barrels per day of oil and 380 million cubic feet of natural gas.
Renaissance earlier reported first-quarter net earnings of C$43.5 million or C$0.36 a share, up from C$34.7 million or C$0.32 a share in the same period last year.
Cash flow in the first three months of 1997 was C$155 million or C$1.27 a share, up from C$125 million or C$1.12 a share.

Woitas said widening spreads between light and heavy oil prices, which have meant big discounts for Canada's growing supply of heavy crude, caused the company to boost its focus on light oil production.

"We're concerned over differentials over the next two to three years. There's just so much supply coming on and in our view there's only so much refining capacity for heavy oil in North America," he said.

At the end of 1996, the company had 10.6 million acres of undeveloped exploration lands in western Canada, a figure Woitas estimated was higher than that of any other company for conventional oil and gas acreage in North America.
He said the land inventory could keep Renaissance drilling for four to five years without property or corporate acquisitions.
"We're full," he said. "Right now, our biggest challenge is understanding all the assets we already have."
